value: ingesting worm eggs passed in droppings
eating earthworms, snails or other hosts carrying worm larvae
wild birds acting as a source of infection
gasping for air with neck stretched out and mouth open
sitting with eyes closed and head drawn back
loss of appetite and refusal to drink in severe cases

mortality.value: Young birds can deteriorate rapidly and die; pheasants can have mortality as high as 25% in outbreaks; adult chickens are usually less severely affected

incubation_period.value: Clinical signs first appear about 1-2 weeks after infection

diagnosis.value: Usually diagnosed from the classic gaping behavior; confirmed at necropsy by finding worms in the trachea or by finding worm eggs in the feces

value: raising young birds in confinement rather than on open range/soil
sanitation and breaking the parasite's life cycle
not raising different species or age groups together

treatment_overview.value: A licensed deworming medication for poultry is used to treat infected birds; ongoing preventive medication is not usually recommended because it is uneconomical and can encourage drug resistance

when_to_call_vet.value: A bird gasping for breath with its neck stretched out and mouth open should be seen quickly, since severe cases can deteriorate and die rapidly.

summary.value: Gapeworm is a parasitic worm that lodges in the windpipe of chickens and other birds, causing gasping and breathing difficulty, especially in young birds. Birds pick it up by eating worm eggs or hosts like earthworms, and it is managed with deworming medication and by keeping young birds off contaminated soil.
